items.title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
items.summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.
items.content:
Image caption, Canada and the US are currently locked in a tit-for-tat trade war
The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.
From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (Â£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".
Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports.
The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".
It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".
Image caption, Maine Senator Susan Collins is seeking to keep her seat in November's midterm elections
Trump "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce", White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said.
Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said: "While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."
The White House's announcement comes less than a fortnight before the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican Party or Democrats will control Congress, impacting the remaining two years of his term.
Collins said she had repeatedly asked senior Trump officials for tariff relief and that she would "continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner".
She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".
Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."
Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war.
Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.
Also on Friday, Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a â trade âdeal with the US.
Carney, who has sought closer ties with Europe since the tariff war erupted, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but was willing to wait it out.
"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC. "If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that."
LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

Ukraine war briefing: Russian diesel tankers headed for North America, says Moscow, as US tries to revive peace talks
Tankers part of US-Russia deal that could see 500,000 metric tonnes of fuel supplied to world market this month. What we know on day 1,704
Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their ⁠way to North America, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak said ⁠on Friday . In ​a statement quoted by Russian news agencies, Novak said the cargoes were ⁠part of a deal that could see Russian companies supply 500,000 metric tonnes to US and world markets in October. “The first ⁠three fuel tankers are already on their ​way to the eastern ‌coast of ‌the Atlantic Ocean, with significant support from the ‌RDIF (Russian Direct Investment Fund),” Novak said. Under a deal announced this month by US president Donald Trump, Russia agreed ‌to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel ​prices in return for Trump temporarily lifting US sanctions on Russian fuel. Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged ⁠medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes, loaded with ultra-low sulphur diesel, is expected to arrive in ‌the US on 7 November.
The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky , where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians. Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations. Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.
The Oleshky ceasefire comes as the US is trying to organise new talks aimed at ending the war . Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US have agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three ⁠countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Zelenskyy said he hoped a meeting of the countries’ leaders would follow.
The peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by Trump seen as favouring Russia, including limitations being placed on the Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem accessing the system, he would straighten it out ​and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
As the UK government prepares next week for the first budget under Andy Burnham’s leadership, EU leaders have pressed the new prime minister at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort . EU officials say Canada and Japan also should do more to support Ukraine .
The UN nuclear watchdog IAEA said ⁠Fiday ​that repairs to key ⁠power infrastructure near Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power ​plant ‌had been completed ‌ under a ‌temporary ceasefire it brokered. The repairs strengthened the plant’s connection ‌to its sole remaining external power ​line, known as Ferosplavna-1, reducing the ⁠risk of another ​loss of ​off-site ​electricity at ​Europe’s largest ‌nuclear ​power ​station.

China is an important trading partner for North Korea and its leader Kim Jong Un [File: AFP]
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge, according to South Korean officials.
The visit on Saturday comes about a week after the bridge linking the two countries was officially opened, 12 years after its completion, deepening economic ties between the Asian giant and its small, nuclear-armed neighbour.

Kim’s visit also comes a day before the anniversary of China joining the 1950–1953 Korean War.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang met Kim in the border city, the Reuters news agency said, quoting a South Korean official.
China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Kim arrived in Dandong through the New Yalu River Bridge connecting the two countries, the Reuters and AFP news agencies reported, quoting unnamed South Korean government officials. South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency also reported the visit, citing an unidentified government source.
Analysts say the visit represents part of Kim’s increasingly assertive foreign policy, as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a “new Cold War”.
Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu River, was a key symbol of strengthening ties between the two countries and reflected their intent to expand trade. It is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks.
The four-lane structure was completed in 2014, but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, according to South Korean news reports.
“The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics,” Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think tank in Shenyang, told Reuters.
“With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further,” Lu said.
China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a vital source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the reclusive state, although ties have not always been smooth.
China, which fought alongside North Korea in the Korean War, is Pyongyang’s main economic and diplomatic backer. However, North Korea has drawn closer to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which analysts say has reduced Pyongyang’s reliance on Beijing.
Kim’s last known visit to China was in September 2025 to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, where he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Xi made a state visit to North Korea in June in which he expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.

Share Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege on social media
Signs of battles between Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis west of Taiz on Wednesday [AFP]
Taiz, Yemen – It was approaching 10:30am in the dialysis centre of the Republican Hospital in Taiz when a machine began filtering excess fluids, toxins and salts from the blood of Omar Mukhtar Hammoud.
The 16-year-old suffers from kidney failure and is one of 270 patients who regularly receive dialysis at the centre in the government-held city in southwest Yemen. But with essential medical supplies and fuel running critically low under the renewed Houthi siege , doctors fear they may soon be unable to provide the treatment that keeps their patients alive.

Dr Essam Mahyoub Dahan, the centre’s director, warned that a complete shutdown could happen within days.
“Because of the siege and the shortage of diesel and medical solutions, we have recently been forced to reduce dialysis sessions from four hours to just two and a half,” Dahan told Al Jazeera. “We know this is not adequate, but we have no choice if we are to keep the centre operating for as long as possible before it shuts down completely.”
Dahan said the centre’s remaining stocks of specialised dialysis solutions were also close to running out.
The supplies, which are expensive, are normally provided by the Yemeni Ministry of Health every three months. But the latest delivery which was due earlier this month  failed to arrive because of the Houthi siege on Taiz city. It began in the first week of October after Houthi advances in the Taiz countryside.
The city was previously under complete Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, in the early years of Yemen’s ongoing war.
Across Taiz governorate, where battles are raging between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iranian-allied Houthi fighters, the number of patients at risk is far greater.
In an October 12 statement, the governorate’s health office warned that the continued siege and obstruction of essential supplies could endanger the lives of 1,110 patients with kidney failure. They depend on dialysis services in the governorate’s hospitals, which collectively provide about 210 dialysis sessions a day.
International humanitarian and health organisations have issued similar warnings about the impact of the siege on the already fragile healthcare system in Taiz.
On Thursday, Amnesty International called on the Houthis to immediately reopen vital roads into and around the city, warning that the closure of the main road between Taiz and the southern port city of Aden threatened hundreds of thousands of civilians with losing access to food, water and healthcare.
Taiz’s hospitals depend heavily on diesel-powered generators because much of the city’s electricity infrastructure was destroyed during the war that began 11 years ago and has not been restored.
The renewed Houthi siege has severely disrupted the entry of fuel, including the diesel needed to run hospital generators and lifesaving medical equipment.
Dr Shaheed al-Ameri, deputy director-general for technical affairs at the Republican Hospital, said the shortages have had a devastating impact on medical services.
“A very large part of this suffering is because of the shortage of diesel,” he told Al Jazeera. “We have no reserve diesel supplies. Our stocks ran out early in the siege and we are now buying it on the black market almost every day, at prices that have reached five times what they were before the siege.”
Al-Ameri warned that the longer the siege continues, the more prices will rise and the further medical services will deteriorate.
The hospital has already suspended operations in some departments, including essential units, he said.
“If this situation continues much longer, we fear we will reach a complete and comprehensive collapse of healthcare services,” he said.
The shortages are not confined to the Republican Hospital. On October 22, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies were threatening lifesaving healthcare throughout  Taiz governorate, with some hospital services already disrupted.
According to the WHO, 42 health facilities in Taiz city had reported severe shortages of essential supplies. Hospitals and ambulances require at least 156,000 litres of fuel a month to continue functioning.
The organisation also warned that diesel shortages threaten to disrupt oxygen production, water pumping, vaccine refrigeration and sanitation services, increasing the risks of disease outbreaks, particularly among displaced families and other vulnerable groups.
The United Nations has separately warned that the restrictions on supplies are bringing Taiz’s health system close to collapse and urged the Houthis to allow humanitarian assistance and essential goods to enter without obstruction.
In its October 12 statement, Taiz’s health office warned that continued restrictions on fuel deliveries could lead to the shutdown of medical oxygen production plants, further endangering patients.
Taysir al-Samei, the health office’s media officer, said that would dramatically worsen the crisis.
“Many medical departments depend on oxygen, particularly operating theatres, inpatient wards, intensive care units and incubators for premature babies,” al-Samei said.
“Most hospitals have already suspended services in some units because of the shortage of diesel and the lack of necessary medical solutions, as well as shortages of medical staff who are struggling to get to work because of the lack of transport,” he added.
He warned that if conditions continued to deteriorate at the same pace, some hospitals could stop providing services in the coming days.
At the Republican Hospital, al-Ameri said that shortages were also affecting diagnostics and treatment. The availability of laboratory reagents had fallen to just 10 to 15 percent of previous levels, he said, while approximately half of the medicines normally available were now out of stock.
Prices for the remaining medicines had doubled, he said, placing them further out of reach for patients already struggling with Yemen’s worsening economic crisis.
The continued fighting and shelling around Taiz have increased the number of wounded people requiring emergency care – placing additional pressure on facilities already struggling with shortages of surgical supplies , anaesthetics and intravenous fluids.
Abdul Badi Abdulwuhab, 53, is another dialysis patient in the Republican Hospital, struggling to cope with the shorter dialysis sessions.
“Because of these measures, I suffer from weakness and I cannot bear the pain,” Abdul Badi told Al Jazeera. “Two and a half hours is not enough to remove all the fluids and toxins from my body.”
Dr Dahan said that the patient’s condition had deteriorated since his sessions were shortened.
“These measures are not effective for many patients,” Dahan said. “The only solution is to end the siege and return things to the way they were.”

Iran ramps up efforts to target US personnel overseas, intelligence memo reveals
A U.S. intelligence memo warns that Iran has intensified efforts to target Americans abroad, with lethal plots reaching "advanced stages" as the State Department adjusts embassy staffing amid escalating security threats in the Middle East.
Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target U.S. personnel abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries, according to an intelligence memo obtained by Fox News.
The memo, sent Friday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, comes just days after the State Department ordered non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia due to escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels .
U.S. officials confirmed the authenticity of the unclassified intelligence memo, which was first reported by Axios.
"Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," the memo states.
'KEEP A LOW PROFILE': STATE DEPARTMENT WARNS AMERICANS OVERSEAS THEY COULD BE TARGETED
Secretary of State Marco Rubio received an intelligence memo warning that Iran had substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel overseas. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AFP)
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," the memo continues.
The memo also states that intelligence officials will work to downgrade the classification of certain intelligence so it can be disseminated and shared with State Department personnel.
A U.S. official told Fox News Digital that the government continually monitors and evaluates evolving security threats.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," the official said. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region."
US PULLS PERSONNEL FROM SAUDI ARABIA AS KINGDOM COMES UNDER HOUTHI FIRE
View of the US State Department before a meeting between Johann Wadephul (CDU), Foreign Minister, and his counterpart, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (Secretary of State). (Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images)
The intelligence report on Iranian efforts to target U.S. diplomats and officials in the Middle East also comes as President Donald Trump continues to weigh another round of military strikes against Iran if Tehran does not reach an agreement with Washington.
Earlier this week, the State Department addressed reports that it directed nonessential government personnel and their dependents to leave the entire Gulf region, clarifying that the departure order applies only to Saudi Arabia.
State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said that any claims of a potential broader regional shutdown were "inaccurate."
AMERICANS WARNED AGAIN TO RETHINK TRAVEL AS MISSILE ATTACK RATTLES HISTORIC REGION
Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid International Airport after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked the airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Reuters)
"The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," the department said.
The State Department previously renewed its warning to Americans traveling in and through the Middle East in late September.
The latest warning came as Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched several missile attacks toward Saudi Arabia .
Fox News Digital's Jessica Mekles and Fox News' Nick Kalman contributed to this report.

Oil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres
Oil has hit its highest level in more than six months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by about 3.5% on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point – its highest level since April.
The jump came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran .
Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.”
The oil price later eased back slight to sit about 2.7% up at just over $116 a barrel. Brent crude had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to touch $126 a barrel by the end of April.
Tensions in the region have been rising this week and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia , which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.
She added: “At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired.”
Streeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.

Saudi Arabia wants to send 10 million barrels of oil a day around Hormuz. A former Treasury official says it may barely move prices
Saudi oil giant Aramco , officially the Saudi Arabian Oil Company, is racing to build a bigger back door around the Strait of Hormuz.
Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said this week that the company is working to raise the capacity of its East-West Crude Oil Pipeline, also known as the Petroline, to 10 million barrels a day from about 7 million today, while running engineering studies on additional export routes. Nasser made the comments to Al Arabiya Business in his first interview since the war began . The plan echoes an announcement earlier this month from Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, who told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh that the expansion would take two to three years .
The goal is to reduce the kingdom’s reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, which has been largely choked off since the U.S. and Israel launched a joint military attack on Iran on Feb. 28. Saudi crude production fell below 7 million barrels a day for much of the war’s first six months, down from more than 10 million before the conflict, and recovered to about 8 million in September, according to the International Energy Agency .
The Petroline spans Saudi Arabia, running roughly 750 miles from the Abqaiq processing hub near the Persian Gulf to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea . Before the war, it typically carried around 2 million barrels a day. Aramco ramped it up within weeks, and the line hit its full 7 million-barrel capacity by late March, with about 2 million of those barrels feeding Saudi refineries rather than export markets. The pipeline helped Aramco post a 25% jump in first-quarter profit . Adding another 3 million barrels a day would be a major undertaking.
But it may have little tangible impact on world fuel prices, according to Gilbert Metcalf , a visiting professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management and a former deputy assistant secretary for environment and energy at the U.S. Treasury Department.
“If—and this is a big if—the Saudis can increase pipeline flow to 10 million barrels per day, it will put about 2% more oil into the global marketplace,” Metcalf tells Fortune . “That could lower prices a bit, but there’s a lot of uncertainty here. The pipeline is vulnerable to drone and missile attacks, as is much of the Saudi petroleum infrastructure. And it’s not entirely clear that there is available refinery capacity to process the oil.”
That vulnerability isn’t hypothetical. The Petroline was first hit in May 2019, when Houthi drones struck a pumping station . This year it has been attacked repeatedly. An April 9 strike on a pumping station cut throughput by about 700,000 barrels a day before Saudi Arabia restored full capacity days later. On Sept. 10, drones struck the line in the Riyadh and Medina regions; Saudi officials said they were launched from Iraq . The attack forced a precautionary shutdown that lasted until Sept. 22, according to Kpler . And a Saudi energy-sector source told AFP that an Oct. 4 attack on a pumping station in Khurais halted flows again , though Bloomberg reported that oil continued to move.
The Red Sea end of the route is under pressure, too. Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, have repeatedly attacked Saudi tankers, and in September seized control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab Strait , the southern gateway to the Red Sea. Southbound tankers leaving Yanbu must pass through it.
Even if the pipeline runs smoothly, a bigger Petroline might do little to ease the world’s dependence on Hormuz. “I don’t think moving more oil to the pipeline takes much pressure off opening the Strait of Hormuz,” Metcalf says. “Despite what the U.S. Treasury and Energy Departments are saying, it does not appear that oil is flowing through Hormuz at anywhere near levels observed before the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran. Add to that threats in the Bab al-Mandab Strait and it’s clear that risks for Saudi oil production are as high now as they’ve ever been.”
Tanker data supports his skepticism. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said this month that Gulf crude flows had recovered to between 80% and 90% of prewar levels. But Kpler figures show oil exports through Hormuz averaged just under 9 million barrels a day in September , roughly 44% of February’s level. Gulf producers are pursuing longer-term workarounds as well: the UAE is fast-tracking a new pipeline of its own .
The Saudi government owns about 81.5% of Aramco. The kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund, holds 16%, and roughly 2.5% trades publicly . It is the world’s largest oil company and a major natural gas producer, with plans to raise gas output 80% by 2030 from 2021 levels. Yet even Aramco’s scale and an expanded pipeline may not be enough to shift the balance of power in the Middle East.
“The irony is that the balance of regional power has tilted from Saudi Arabia towards Iran as a result of the attacks on Iran,” Metcalf says. “This would have been unthinkable just a year ago.”

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Waves generated by Typhoon Champi crash against a seawall in Keelung. Photograph: Ann Wang/Reuters Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

items.content:
Trump Invokes Cold War-Era Law to Boost Oil Refining as Gas Prices Soar
President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era defense law to direct up to $150 million toward U.S. oil refineries as gasoline prices climb above $4 a gallon and diesel exceeds $6. The October 22 action allows the federal government to support refinery expansion and petroleum infrastructure projects under powers intended to protect national defense.
The administration's plan draws on a broader $1 billion congressional allocation for energy projects considered critical to national security. The Department of Energy expects the investments to add millions of gallons of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel to daily domestic production, although funding recipients and project timelines have yet to be announced.
Trump signed a presidential memorandum directing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to use Section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950 to strengthen domestic petroleum production, refining, pipelines and fuel storage facilities. The order identifies those operations as essential to national defense and authorizes federal purchases, financial commitments and agreements to expand industrial capacity.
The directive comes as global energy disruptions linked to the conflict involving Iran and attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to pressure fuel markets. As of October 23, the national average price of gasoline stood at approximately $4.29 per gallon, while diesel averaged $6.32, increasing transportation and operating costs for consumers and businesses.
Trump determined that financing constraints, construction timelines, permitting delays and supply chain limitations have prevented private industry from expanding petroleum infrastructure quickly enough to meet national defense needs. Trump cited the risk of a petroleum shortfall that could severely impair national defense capabilities.
The president also waived six statutory requirements governing federal support for industrial expansion, citing the national energy emergency he declared in January 2025. Section 303 of the Defense Production Act allows the government to support industries essential to national defense through purchases, financial commitments and investments in production capacity. Enacted during the Korean War, the statute permits specified requirements to be waived during a declared national emergency or when an industrial shortage threatens defense capabilities.
Trump previously invoked the same provision on April 20, designating domestic petroleum production, refining and distribution as essential to national defense. That determination assigned implementation to the energy secretary, while the October 22 memorandum directs Hegseth to carry out the authority.
The Energy Department's latest funding initiative would support efforts to restore and expand American refineries. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the funding would help restart and expand U.S. refining operations.
Federal funding could accelerate expansions at existing refineries, although industry specialists expect substantial increases in fuel production to take months. Equipment purchases, construction and regulatory approvals remain among the obstacles facing operators.
Any relief at the pump could take longer. Gasoline and diesel prices remain tied to global crude oil costs and supply disruptions, limiting how quickly expanded U.S. refining operations could affect what consumers pay.
The Energy Department has yet to identify funding recipients or establish a timeline for the refinery expansions. Project selections will be the next step in determining how quickly the administration's $150 million initiative translates into additional fuel production.

items.title: Turmoil hits AI buildout as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
items.summary: Stock slumps, pulled IPOs and rising spreads on credit default swaps this week sets stage for hyperscaler earnings.
items.content:
AI turmoil: neoclouds struggle, credit risks jump, Solidigm pulls IPO
Concerns over the AI trade dragged the Nasdaq down this week, with neoclouds posting some of the steepest losses.
Debt markets are roiling, with Meta, Oracle and Nvidia facing the largest-ever spreads on credit default swaps linked to their corporate bonds.
SK Hynix abandoned plans for an IPO of its Solidigm unit.
CoreWeave founder and CEO Mike Intrator poses for a photo during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq headquarters in New York, March 28, 2025.
Neoclouds tanked. Credit default swaps soared. Meta turned cash flow negative. And SK Hynix's Solidigm unit canceled plans for its initial public offering.
It's been a rocky week for the AI infrastructure trade.
The Nasdaq followed Thursday's beating with an additional drop on Friday to end the week down 0.7%. Among the hyperscalers, the worst performer was Alphabet , shares of which sank 6% ahead of the internet giant's third-quarter earnings report next week. Microsoft and Amazon are also on the docket, and they each saw shares fall less than 1%.
While the tech market has thus far avoided a dramatic across-the-board sell-off, the artificial intelligence buildout is showing signs of strain.
Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN all fell sharply this week, bringing their losses for October to well over 30% each. CoreWeave, the leader of the pack, has seen spreads on its CDS widen past 11%, generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default.
Meanwhile, yields on the company's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes topped 15% .
"What investors are doing is throwing every baby out with the bathwater and saying anyone who is a neocloud" will be devalued, Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday.
Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza on the problem with neoclouds
Fears aren't limited to the U.S. market. Shares of Elice Group, a South Korean cloud provider, dropped 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, and shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast.
AI optimism has been the major market driver for the past couple of years, as unrelenting demand for new models and services pushes the world's biggest tech companies to spend on infrastructure at historic rates. However, skeptics are getting more vocal in their concerns that returns on AI investment won't justify the capital expenditures.
Analysts at research and advisory firm Gartner predict that 80% of neocloud companies will either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , perhaps the leading AI evangelist, remains bullish. Huang said this week at a company conference in Berlin that "demand for the neoclouds is off the charts."
"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal . "That's going to get solved."
Wall Street isn't convinced. On Thursday, South Korean memory giant SK Hynix , one of the biggest winners in the AI boom, said it's pulling an IPO for its U.S.-based Solidigm unit, citing market volatility. SK Hynix purchased Solidigm, which makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers, from Intel in 2021.
"While an IPO was expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns, the review has been discontinued in light of market conditions and share price trends," SK Hynix said in a release .
Despite the turmoil, all of tech's mega-caps have maintained their investment-grade rating even as they've opened their wallets to fuel their build-outs, including through debt. Even with that group of companies, the market is showing some jitters.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026.
Meta saw its stock plunge 7% on Thursday after the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter of over $2 billion while raising the floor of its full-year capex to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on various leases and contracts, with over $450 billion of those leases being non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements.
Spreads on Meta's five-year CDS reached all-time highs of over 124 basis points. CDS on Nvidia and Oracle also touched records, with their spreads hitting 126 basis points and 343 basis points, respectively, this week. Oracle's stock has lost over one-third of its value this year, and now the company faces risks of a credit rating downgrade .
John Williams, who leads the derivatives practice at law firm Milbank LLP, says investors are seeking numerous ways beyond buying CDS to hedge their bets with respect to the AI trade.
"There's so much investment going into it that it's just very appropriate to look for risk management tools, completely regardless of whether you're bullish or bearish," Williams said. "It would be crazy for people not to be looking for appropriate risk management tools for it."
Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, told CNBC's "SquawkBox Asia" last week that it's "all kind of tied together," referring to AI's impact on the whole market.
"Can you drop a bowling ball in one part of the pool and not get any waves downstream to the rest of the Nasdaq?" he said. "I don't know. I have some concern about that."
— CNBC's Katie Tarasov contributed to this report

items.summary: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?  The Guardian
items.content:
Residents sit at a viewing platform overlooking the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters
Residents sit at a viewing platform overlooking the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters
North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?
Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons
For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.
Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia.
map The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.
It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border , named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.
map “China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.
Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to support Vladimir Putin ’s war in Ukraine, and has held two summits with the Russian president in the past three years. In 2024, the leaders signed a mutual defence pact that includes a clause requiring the countries to come to each other’s aid if attacked.
Trucks adorned with Chinese flags cross the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge into North Korea’s Sinuiju.
Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters In return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the opportunity to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional ally China .
North Korea stands to benefit from increased trade but for China, the bridge could be of more geopolitical value than economic given how little trade China does with its neighbour compared with its other partners.
However, the insular regime in Pyongyang is thought to be reluctant to increase its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing’s previous support for UN sanctions targeting the North’s nuclear weapons programme .
In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese support for UN sanctions has collapsed. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University. “However, because China’s enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).”
The newly opened New Yalu River Bridge could be of more geopolitical importance than economic for China. Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters The North’s “open” border with China contrasts dramatically with the one it shares with South Korea. In 2024, the North said it would sever all rail and road links with its neighbour, months after Kim said he would abandon the goal of peaceful reunification and declared South Korea his country’s “ principal enemy ”.
But Fyodor Tertitskiy, a North Korea expert at Korea University in Seoul, believes neither China nor Russia can influence North Korea in any meaningful way, citing Kim’s refusal to surrender his nuclear weapons or moderate his iron grip on power – two changes that would be welcomed in Moscow and Beijing.
“Both countries understand that Kim Jong-un would rather accept a complete breakdown in relationships than submit,” he says. “So I doubt we are seeing a straightforward struggle for influence. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.”
Kim is more likely to turn to China improve his country’s struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. China may seek to recover lost influence by increasing trade and people-to-people exchanges, but the Kim regime prizes autonomy and wants to limit foreign ideological and cultural influences.”
The South Korean government said last year that at least 17 active road and rail links connect North Korea and China along their 1,400 km-long border.
Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence. Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters Tertitskiy is “not particularly optimistic” that the increased contact the bridges will bring means improvements to the lives of ordinary North Koreans or lead to a more western-style economy. “I think it will make reform even less likely. Why pursue reforms and take risks when you can just get what you need from abroad?”
Analysts say the expected rise in trade across the Yalu bridge is likely to be modest at first. But it could become a bellwether for the state of Sino-North Korean ties, says Easley.
“China remains economically indispensable to North Korea in ways that Russia cannot replace,” he says, adding, “In that sense, the bridge may offer an inadvertent window into bilateral relations if flows are visibly interrupted in the future.”

French police make 135 arrests as protests take place across Europe – Europe live
France has deployed 70,000 officers around the country, while Italian police have raided homes in Milan, with protests also under way in Spain and Albania
Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.15 EDT First published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 04.14 EDT
French police make 135 arrests, interior minister says
'Here to support the schoolchildren's demands'
Paris protest route moved away from Bastille and pushed back to afternoon
Some protest bans overturned in last-minute court challenges
Drive-by shooting outside of Paris targeted victims on skin colour
A protest march in Orléans, where Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party is holding its congress. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images
A protest march in Orléans, where Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party is holding its congress. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images
France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has said that police have made 135 arrests in relation to the nationwide protests, and seized a variety of weapons.
Weapons confiscated included metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, Nuñez said. He added that, so far, “there has been no major incident”.
Police conducting security checks in the Place de la République, Paris, on Saturday. Photograph: Mouneb Taim/Anadolu/Getty Images
French police make 135 arrests, interior minister says
'Here to support the schoolchildren's demands'
Paris protest route moved away from Bastille and pushed back to afternoon
Some protest bans overturned in last-minute court challenges
Drive-by shooting outside of Paris targeted victims on skin colour
An anti-government rally is taking place in the Albanian capital, Tirana, after days of violent unrest in the city.
Protesters have been calling for the prime minister, Edi Rama, to resign since last week, and demanding action against corruption and poor living standards. More than 300 people have been injured in the protests amid clashes with police, with dozens of demonstrators detained and damage to government buildings.
Protesters outside the prime ministers’s office in the Albanian capital, Tirana. Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/AP “There is a lot of anger,” activist Sidorela Vatnikaj told AFP, labelling the movement a “revolution”.
“It’s not a matter of only students, it’s not a matter only of environmental struggles ... It’s a matter of the state of rights and state of law.”
AFP is reporting that police in Lyon, south-east France , fired teargas to disperse about 150 protesters near the city centre – where demonstrations had been banned – when they briefly tried to block a road.
A 21-year-old student, speaking anonymously, told AFP: “The police are really mobile ... They come and disperse marches before they even form.”
Demonstrators are on the move in Orléans, where Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party is holding its congress.
Thousands of people are marching, Agence France-Presse reports, shouting anti-fascist slogans and calling for Le Pen to be imprisoned, and for the French president, Emmanuel Macron , to resign. Police put the number of marchers at 11,000, while organisers said 26,000 took part.
The protest march in Orléans. Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/Reuters The Guardian’s Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis has been speaking with more demonstrators in the French capital.
Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant , said he was demonstrating to support young people’s demands for improvements in education.
I think young people need to take part in building the future they will live in. I have an eight-year-old granddaughter, I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands and feelings.
Pierre, 60, with his messages: “The young people are waiting for responses to their demands” and “Mr. President, France is speaking to you, listen to us” Photograph: Angelique Chrisafis/The Guardian Emma, 35, a science podcaster, was protesting for the second Saturday.
I want to be part of a mass of people standing up for the schoolchildren protestors and saying the misery of the few is the concern of us all. I feel anger and despair at the rise of fascism and misery in the world and I want people to unite to campaign for something better.
Paris protester Emma holding a sign that reads: “The suffering of a few is the concern of all”. Photograph: Angelique Chrisafis/The Guardian Further student and youth demonstrations across the political spectrum are expected in Italian cities today after major anti-government protests kicked off last weekend.
Like in France , several of those demonstrations at times spiralled into looting and clashes with police.
Prime Minister Georgia Meloni – deeply unpopular with many young people – has deployed 500 extra soldiers to Milan and announced harsher penalties for minors, after major looting there last week.
Police said the ransacking in Milan had involved about 2,000 youths. Police have stepped up ID checks at railway stations and deployed surveillance drones.
500 soldiers from the ‘Folgore’ Parachute Brigade, one of the Italian Army’s elite units, have been deployed to patrol Milan’s central sites Photograph: Andrea Carrubba/Anadolu/Getty Images In Rome, authorities have also stepped up patrols and shut down luxury shopping strips and are restricting access around t he Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.
Right-wing students have been staging a demonstration this morning, in response to largely left-wing protests held last week which railed against Meloni’s government and called for better schools, affordable housing and cost-of-living measures.
An anti-war protest is also scheduled in a few hours time at Piazza della Repubblica.
Members of right-wing student groups marched through the streets of Rome this morning in a rally organized in opposition to recent left-wing student protests Photograph: Gregorio Borgia/AP
Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, joining the street march on October 24 2026 Photograph: Angelique Chrisafis/The Guardian Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, had turned out for the street march.
She said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them and we have to stand together.”
She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war… This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”
Police in Italy have raided 150 homes in Milan and other cities as the country braces for more protests on Saturday afternoon.
The searches were conducted in the homes of those, including 51 minors, suspected of intending to cause trouble during the demonstrations.
The events, organised by the 17 October Movement and due to take place in Milan, Turin, Rome, Bologna, Naples and other cities and towns, are targeted at various issues, from the high cost of living and underfunding in schools to support for Palestine.
They follow protests last weekend which escalated into violence, especially in Milan, where hooded youths vandalised and looted shops in the city centre.
Many stores in Milan, Naples and other cities have covered windows with plywood over fears of further violence on Saturday.
A boarded-up Prada store in Naples, Italy. Photograph: Ciro De Luca/Reuters Late last night, Paris police also ordered a change in the route for the main march that’s been organised by trade unions.
Originally, protesters had been given the green-light to march from Bastille to Nation squares in the centre, with the rally to commence in the late morning.
However, in their decree banning the route , police said such a procession presented “ serious risks of public disorder, particularly due to the high density of businesses similar to those targeted during the 17-18 October weekend.”
French riot police officers patrolling Place de la Bastille this morning. The historic square, a symbol of the French Revolution, was the centre of protests last weekend Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPA Demonstrators can now only march from Porte de Vincennes and Porte d’Italie from 1pm to 7pm. Organisers had scrambled a legal challenge but that has failed, and groups are now preparing for a 2pm start.
The new route is on the outskirts of the Parisian ring, through the 13th and 12th arrondisements.
Paris’s streets are pretty quiet at the moment. Police are out in full force guarding the main squares and government buildings, metro stations are closed, and most retail shops are closed or about to shut up shop.
A police officer stands in front of a boarded-up Sephora store. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters View image in fullscreen
Police vehicles parked in front of the Arc de Triomphe Photograph: Emma Da Silva/AP Following last weekend’s unrest, authorities across France moved to try to restrict demonstrations, limiting gathering numbers and march routes and issuing blanket bans in some cities.
That led to groups seeking permission for “authorised” protests with mixed results. For example, in Paris, the leading trade union was granted permission for their march while the Yellow Vest demonstrators were denied.
The bans have also sparked last-minute legal challenges from civil rights groups.
And now in the past hour, courts have overturned two protest bans – in the Bouches-du-Rhône prefecture and its capital Marseille and also in the city of Limoges , which saw its centuries-old city hall set on fire last week.
Other cities that have bans in place for “unauthorised” demonstrations include:
Paris, Lille, Strasbourg, Mulhouse, Grenoble, Toulouse, Amiens
Of course, many protesters – from students to union groups – have said they will march anyway regardless of the bans or rules around where and when they can demonstrate.
The mood in Paris was heightened by fear and horror after what the government said was “racist, terrorist attack” in two towns west of the city on Friday.
A 26-year-old, well-respected martial arts star from a club outside Paris was killed and five other people were injured, including a 12-year-old girl shot eight times as a gunman pointed an automatic weapon from his car.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron , said they were targeted because of the colour of their skin.
“These people were targeted because of their skin color or perceived religion, and for no other reason,” he said during his visit to Trappes, one of the affected towns, on Friday afternoon. “There is no place for this in France .”
Macron met community members at the Trappes town hall after a drive-by shooting during which a person was killed and at least four others were wounded including a 12-year-old girl Photograph: McKay Hannah/ABACA/Shutterstock “There are no words,” wrote the sports club of the 26-year-old victim, the ATCH Academy. “Nothing could justify a life being torn away like this.”
Several of France’s leftwing political leaders have already shown up at the rallies in Orléans protesting against Marine Le Pen and her anti-immigrant party.
The demonstrations against “racism, fascism and imperialism” are being held as the National Rally’s congress takes place this weekend and Le Pen launches her presidential campaign.
“It was important for me to come here to Orléans,” said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis , saying he was there to stand up against racism and the hate speech spread by the right.
He also directly referenced the “close link” between hateful rhetoric from parties like Le Pen’s, and the drive-by shooting outside of Paris on Friday morning which the town’s mayor had said appeared to be targeting people of African origin.
Sophie Binet, General Secretary of the CGT union , also began her address to protesters by addressing the Trappes attack.
I want to express our support and condolences to the victims, their families, and all the residents of Trappes.
This violence does not come from nowhere, it comes from speeches that convey racism, anti-Semitism, violence, which essentially come from the speeches of the far right .
The Socialist party leader, Olivier Faure , has also been seen in the crowds, marching behind an “All united against fascism” banner.
Tension was also high in the city of Orléans on Saturday as Marine Le Pen’s far-right, anti-immigration National Rally party gathers for its annual congress and the official launch of her presidential campaign.
The police presence in the city has been stepped up as around 5,000 party members and officials gather on Saturday and 10,000 attend Le Pen’s first campaign rally on Sunday.
A protest march by the left has been organised against “racism, fascism and imperialism”. Between 20,000 and 30,000 people are expected to demonstrate against the far right in the city.
Several political personalities on the left were to attend the Orléans march including the leader of the Socialist party, Olivier Faure, the head of the leftwing CGT union, Sophie Binet, and the mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko , from the party La France Insoumise.
The capital’s authorities have shut down the stations in a bid to contain crowds and curb movement throughout the city today.
The affected stations are: Argentine, Assemblée Nationale, Bel Air, Champs-Elysées – Clemenceau, Charles de Gaulle – Étoile, Cluny - La Sorbonne, Concorde, Daumesnil, Dugommier, Franklin D. Roosevelt, George V, Mabillon, Maubert – Mutualité, Miromesnil, Odéon, Picpus, Rennes, Rue du Bac, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Saint-Sulpice, Sèvres - Babylone, Solférino, Tuileries and Varenne.
We’ve seen other attempts by authorities to restrict movement in cities across France for this weekend; Marseille authorities earlier this week said they would suspend public transport services on Saturday; they were forced to reverse the decision following outcry.
In Orléans , which is hosting the far-right National Rally congress, the tram lines are suspended and bike-sharing rentals have been removed from the city centre.
A jogger runs past a Societe Generale bank branch with its storefronts protected by wooden panels on the Champs-Elysees avenue in Paris ahead of nationwide protests on
October 24, 2026. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters All through the night in neighbourhoods in the centre and east of Paris, the sound of sawing, drilling and hammering rang out as wooden boards were hastily secured into place to cover windows and shop-fronts.
Businesses being boarded up included opticians, supermarkets and pharmacies as well as trainers and handbag stores.
Hundreds of shops were smashed and looted over two nights last weekend in Paris, and thousands more in cities across France , including Marseille and Bordeaux.
At a public meeting at Paris city hall this week, some shop-owners had cried as they spoke of their fears of businesses being smashed and looted again this weekend.
“I’m afraid there isn’t enough wooden board left to protect shops and the demand is making it so expensive to board up shops,” one optician near Châtelet in the city centre said. “We’ll close up and take all our stock of glasses out of the shop.”
Workers install wooden panels to protect the windows of the gaming club Partouche Pasino Club in Paris Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in Europe – we will be closely following protests across the continent today.
In France , hundreds of thousands are expected at rallies across the country, with high school students, unionists, “yellow vest” demonstrators and others turning out for a fourth weekend of protests demanding more government funding for schools and measures to help with housing and the cost of living.
Desperate to avoid the looting and property damage seen on the fringes of some protests last weekend, French authorities have ramped up restrictions on where protesters can march and which groups are “authorised” to do so. They’ve increased policing 20%, mobilising 70,000 police officers and soldiers to the streets, including both elite units and trainee officers.
Many of Paris’s metro stations and major museums and tourist sites are shut today, while across the country, shops and businesses have been urged to close their doors.
Community tensions are also high following a deadly shooting on Friday west of Paris where the gunman targeted non-white people, killing one person and injuring five others including a child. The French president called it a “racist terrorist attack”.
Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s anti-immigration party is also due to hold its national conference in the central city of Orléans. The far-right National Rally’s meeting is expected to draw up to 30,000 counter-demonstrators.
Protests are also being held in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland today.

items.content:
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
Hezbollah is leveraging several political and informational lines of effort to deter the Lebanese government from prosecuting the group for a recent smuggling operation, which Hezbollah likely fears could establish a precedent for legal action against its illicit activities.
Hezbollah’s lines of effort are indicative of the challenges that face the government as it attempts to confront Hezbollah but do not guarantee that Hezbollah will succeed in breaking the government's will to disarm and prosecute the group in this instance.
Iraq-based Axis of Resistance actors have very likely launched at least four drones targeting Saudi Arabia within the past 20 days. Attacks on Saudi Arabia and other regional countries from Iraq by any Iranian partner or proxy support Iranian objectives to compel the United States to end the war in terms favorable to Iran by imposing increasing costs on US partners and allies in the region.
Saudi Arabia is expanding the scope of its air campaign in Yemen by interdicting Houthi smuggling cargo that could sustain Houthi military activities against the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia.
Hezbollah is leveraging several political and informational lines of effort to deter the Lebanese government from prosecuting the group for a recent smuggling operation, which Hezbollah likely fears could establish a precedent for legal action against its illicit activities. The Lebanese government is investigating the group after Lebanese Internal Security Forces (ISF) personnel interdicted a Hezbollah truck carrying nearly 800 kilograms of high explosives from the Bekaa Valley to Beirut's southern suburbs on October 5.[1] The government currently seeks to refer the criminal case to the Judicial Council, which is Lebanon's highest criminal court, and prosecute the Hezbollah members involved in smuggling explosives.[2] Referring the case to the Judicial Council would break Hezbollah’s de facto legal immunity and expose the organization to potential legal consequences.[3] Hezbollah accordingly likely views the possible legal actions that the government is exploring as steps that could progress or even hasten existing government efforts to disarm the group entirely under the June 2026 Agreement, particularly by establishing a precedent for legal action against Hezbollah’s illicit activities.[4] Lebanese government success in holding Hezbollah accountable for smuggling weapons threatens Hezbollah’s ability to resupply itself with impunity and maintain its arms.[5] The successful prosecution of the case could also strengthen the government’s confidence and preparedness to further challenge Hezbollah’s military and criminal activities, potentially to the point of military disarmament.
Hezbollah is attempting to exploit the Lebanese government’s sensitivity toward civil conflict by threatening the government with unrest and portraying the government as sectarian and beholden to Israeli interests. Hezbollah’s parliamentary bloc warned on October 23 that Lebanon is liable to “fragmentation” and suggested that the government is pushing Lebanon toward civil conflict in pursuing legal action against Hezbollah.[6] Hezbollah officials further derided the government’s efforts as “settling internal sectarian scores.”[7] The Hezbollah officials also called any attempt to arrest Hezbollah officials an “act of Israeli aggression,” which is likely also a veiled threat to confront government police or military action.[8] Hezbollah has historically used these kinds of threats and rhetoric to render the Lebanese government and public unwilling to threaten the group’s military organization.[9] The government is particularly sensitive to such threats given Lebanon’s history of civil war and sectarian violence.[10]
Hezbollah also leveraged its political alliance with Parliament Speaker and Hezbollah ally Nabih Berri, who leads the Shia Amal Movement, to delay President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam’s efforts to prosecute Hezbollah on October 22.[11] Lebanese media reported on October 23 that Berri urged Aoun and Salam to postpone a necessary cabinet vote that would refer the Hezbollah explosives case to the Judicial Council, which answers to the pro-government Justice Minister and issues binding rulings without appeal.[12] Berri reportedly promised Aoun and Salam that, in return for postponing the cabinet vote, Hezbollah would neither foment civil conflict nor trigger a government crisis by withdrawing Hezbollah and Amal from the cabinet.[13] The Lebanese ISF and Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) will continue to investigate the incident during this postponement under the Lebanese Military Court’s jurisdiction.[14] The Military Court is led by Brigadier General Wassim Fayad, who is reportedly close to Hezbollah and has previously obstructed prosecutions under pressure from the group.[15]
Hezbollah’s lines of effort illustrate the challenges facing the Lebanese government as it attempts to confront the group, but these efforts do not guarantee that Hezbollah will succeed in breaking the government's will to disarm and prosecute the group in this instance. Hezbollah is relying on lines of effort that have succeeded during previous efforts to hold the group accountable over the last two decades.[16] Hezbollah is far weaker and less popular now than it was during some of these previous efforts, however, because it has exhausted much of its military strength and popular support since October 2023 by initiating destructive wars with Israel.[17] The Lebanese government is also demonstrating resolve to counter Hezbollah’s threats and thwart its illicit activities, including by authorizing ISF raids and LAF deployments in Beirut’s southern suburbs, which are a historical Hezbollah stronghold.[18] ISW-CTP has outlined Hezbollah’s lines of effort to avoid disarmament and vulnerabilities that the United States and Lebanon can exploit in an October 22 special report (read the full report here: How Hezbollah is Preventing its Disarmament, Again .)[19]
Saudi Arabia is expanding the scope of its air campaign in Yemen by interdicting Houthi smuggling cargo that could sustain Houthi military operations against the internationally recognized Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia.[20] Saudi coalition aircraft reportedly struck a likely Houthi smuggling vessel near Houthi-controlled Zuqar Island in the Red Sea on October 22.[21] Saudi coalition aircraft have increasingly targeted Houthi smuggling vessels in the Red Sea since October 16.[22] The Saudi Joint Forces Command also issued a statement warning Yemeni vessels against supporting Houthi smuggling efforts on October 19.[23] The Houthis have established an extensive international smuggling network, with support from the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC), to acquire small arms, drone and missile components, and other military equipment in recent years.[24] Saudi interdiction efforts likely aim to prevent arms and equipment that the Houthis could use to resupply frontline units from reaching the group by interdicting vessels carrying illicit cargo. The Houthis could also theoretically use drone and missile equipment acquired through smuggling to supply Houthi missile and drone units that are conducting daily attacks on Saudi critical infrastructure (see below).
The increase in Saudi airstrikes targeting Houthi smuggling assets comes amid challenges to the Yemeni government’s ability to conduct maritime counter-smuggling operations. The Yemeni-government-aligned, Saudi-backed National Resistance Forces historically relied upon its positions on the Red Sea coast, and at Mokha port in particular, as a base for the Yemeni government's maritime counter-smuggling operations in the Red Sea. The Houthis seized this coastline, including Mokha, on September 10.[25] The loss of Yemeni-controlled territory and port infrastructure along the Red Sea coast has almost certainly limited the Yemeni government's ability to conduct anti-smuggling operations against the Houthis.[26] It is also unclear if government forces have had the bandwidth to conduct such counter-smuggling operations while forces are currently engaged in a full mobilization against the Houthis.

Degrade the US ability and willingness to continue the war
Restore deterrence vis- à -vis the United States and its regional partners
Divide the United States and Israel from the Arab states
Iraq-based Axis of Resistance actors have very likely launched at least four drones targeting Saudi Arabia within the past 20 days.[27] Saudi security sources told US-funded regional media on October 22 that the drones targeted unspecified “vital sites.”[28] Saudi Arabia has reportedly informed the Iraqi federal government of the attacks.[29] The report did not specify where in Iraq the launches originated, but Iraqi authorities have reportedly increased surveillance over militia sites in Maysan Province over the past two weeks that they suspect Iranian-backed Iraqi militias are using to conduct attacks.[30] IRGC-managed Iraqi militia cells based along the Iraq-Iran border, including in Maysan Province, have conducted multiple attacks on neighboring countries in recent months, including a September 10 attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline.[31] The Houthis, who maintain an active presence in Iraq, reportedly coordinated some of these cross-border attacks with Iraqi militias.[32] It is possible that Iraqi fighters, Houthi fighters, or a combination of Iraqi and Houthi forces launched the drones at Saudi Arabia. Attacks on Saudi Arabia and other regional countries from Iraq by any Iranian partner or proxy support Iranian objectives to compel the United States to end the war in terms favorable to Iran by imposing increasing costs on US partners and allies in the region, including by imposing economic costs through attacks on energy infrastructure.
Yemeni government-aligned forces continued to advance into contested territory south of Taiz City, likely to try to break the Houthis’ encirclement of government-aligned forces in central Taiz Governorate. Yemeni government-aligned forces advanced to Jabal Manara in al Misrakh District on October 22, which the Houthis previously occupied, according to Yemeni and DC-based Yemen analyst sources.[33] Yemeni government-aligned forces have advanced into al Misrakh District and engaged Houthi fighters in the area in recent days, likely in order to try to break the Houthis' encirclement of central Taiz Governorate. The Houthis fully encircled the city on October 12.[34]
Yemeni government-aligned forces’ advances into al Misrakh District come amid the continued success of Yemeni government-aligned forces’ efforts to repel Houthi advances into the “Old Airport” neighborhood on the western outskirts of Taiz City on October 22.[35] Yemeni government-aligned forces similarly repelled Houthi attempts to advance into the area on October 17 and 18.[36] The “Old Airport” neighborhood sits along a major road leading into Taiz City that the Houthis have sought to capture in recent weeks.[37]
The Houthis have continued to attack targets across Saudi Arabia to impose economic and political costs on Saudi Arabia and compel Saudi Arabia to capitulate to Houthi demands. The Saudi Joint Forces Command reported that Saudi air defenses intercepted one ballistic missile over Najran, southern Saudi Arabia, on October 22.[38] Saudi air defenses also intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh and Khamis Mushait and two drones over Saudi Arabia’s southern region on October 23.[39] The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil facilities, airports, and other civilian infrastructure as part of their ongoing strike campaign to compel Saudi Arabia to halt military operations against the Houthis and accept the Houthis’ demands, which include lifting Saudi controls on Houthi-controlled ports and airports and granting the Houthis control over Yemen’s oil and gas resources.[40]
