Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 23, 2026
Ukrainian officials are widely reporting continued in-motion speed restrictions on SpaceX’s low-earth orbit satellite communication technology (Starlink and Starshield) on October 23, but the situation remains unclear. Ukrainian sources, including the Ukrainian General Staff and sources within the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (MoD), reported on October 23 that Ukrainian forces have observed “cases of connection loss” in Starlink/Starshield terminal operations at speeds of 161 kilometers per hour (around 100 miles per hour).[1] Sources within the Ukrainian MoD stated that there has been “no confirmation” about the removal of in-motion speed restrictions.[2] Ukrainian defense minister Serhii Sternenko stated that the situation with Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions “remains ambiguous” since some Ukrainian units report the resumption of operations at speeds exceeding the previously established limits, but the resumption does not apply to all missions, and he noted that some disruptions continue.[3] The situation regarding in-motion Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions remains unclear, but Ukrainian sources are emphasizing that Ukrainian forces continue experiencing problems with accessing Starlink/Starshield terminals as of October 23.
Russia and Ukraine have reportedly agreed to a limited ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast. The White House reported on October 23 that US First Lady Melania Trump secured a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in Russia-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast beginning on October 29 to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation from the city amid a dire humanitarian crisis.[4] Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on October 23 the White House’s press release and noted that Ukraine and Russia agreed to conduct a humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky, including securing a limited ceasefire, delivering humanitarian cargo to the city, and ensuring the free movement of civilians from the settlement.[5] Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov confirmed on October 23 that Russia agreed to the limited ceasefire in the Kherson direction beginning at 0400 local Moscow time on October 27 — a notably different start date from the one given in the White House press release.[6]
Russian occupation authorities are fully responsible for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky and have repeatedly and deliberately blocked evacuation and humanitarian routes into the settlement since the beginning of Russia's occupation.[7] Russian occupation authorities stopped the delivery of food and other critical supplies into Oleshky in late December 2025 and have failed to deliver any food or medicine to Oleshky since May 2026. The Kremlin rejected three local humanitarian ceasefire proposals from Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in May, July, and September 2026, after which Ukrainian forces conducted an operation to provide food to Oleshky residents via drone drops in September 2026.[8] Russian authorities have long refused to address the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, and Gerasimov’s October 23 statement is the first instance of a Russian attempt to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin articulated his long-standing commitment to wider territorial aims in Ukraine far beyond Donetsk Oblast by invoking mythologized and false Russian “historical claims”. Putin claimed on October 22 that occupied Ukraine is “the territory of historical Russia” while rejecting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s October 21 proposal to freeze the current frontline as part of a ceasefire agreement.[9] Putin also claimed that the “latest genetic research” identifies Russians and Ukrainians as “one people.” Putin’s October 22 reference to “historical Russia” likely refers to "Novorossiya" — an amorphous invented region in southern and eastern Ukraine that the Kremlin has claimed is “integral” to Russia.[10] Novorossiya notably includes not only Crimea and the four oblasts that Russia has illegally annexed (Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts), but also Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa oblasts.[11] Putin’s invocation of Russia’s historical claims demands that Ukraine surrender the Ukrainian-controlled 20.5 percent of Donetsk Oblast, 24.5 percent of Zaporizhia Oblast, including Zaporizhzhia City with a pre-war population of over 700,000 people, and 30 percent of Kherson Oblast, including Kherson City with a pre-war population of nearly 300,000 people. Putin’s October 23 statement explicitly demonstrates that Russian demands extend far beyond Ukraine’s Fortress Belt and Donetsk Oblast and may include the entire territory of Ukraine . Putin also emphasized his commitment to achieving all Russian war goals, which include the Russian demand for Ukraine’s full capitulation.[12] Putin’s statement demonstrates that the Kremlin is willing to participate in “negotiations” with Ukraine solely for the purpose of accepting Kyiv's surrender — not for the purpose of coming to some compromise peace agreement.
Putin also agreed to discuss the “European security architecture as a whole” after ensuring Ukraine’s and Russia’s future security.[13] Putin’s comment on “revising” the European security architecture refers to another Russian long-standing demand first articulated in the December 2021 ultimatum preceding the full-scale invasion that includes halting the deployment of military forces and weapons systems to NATO states that joined the alliance after 1997 and granting Russia a veto over certain NATO exercises.[14] Putin’s December 2021 demands are incompatible with US President Donald Trump’s commitment to maintaining a US military presence in Poland and the current US troop deployments in the Baltic States.
The Kremlin appears to be increasingly adopting a more cautious monetary policy amid continued inflationary pressures, which may pose risks to wage growth and Russia’s defense industrial base (DIB). The Russian Central Bank announced on October 23 that it would keep the key interest rate at 14 percent for the second consecutive month, after lowering the rate 10 times over the past 18 months, citing elevated price pressure and high inflation expectations.[15] The Central Bank’s baseline scenario assumes an average key interest rate of 12.5 to 13.5 percent in 2027 — only 0.5 to 1.5 percentage points below the current rate. The Central Bank noted that underlying price growth is “not slowing” and identified pro-inflationary risks (or risk factors that increase inflation over the medium term), including price growth between five and six percent and estimated annual inflation of 6.8 percent. The Central Bank estimated that annual inflation will range between 7.1 and 7.6 percent by the end of 2026, a slight increase from the Central Bank’s September 11 announcement, and noted that volatile items like motor fuel (an oblique reference to the effects of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure) will continue impacting price dynamics. Russian Central Bank Chairwoman Elvira Nabiullina stated on October 23 that supply and demand continue facing inflationary risks, elevated inflation expectations, labor market tensions, and a larger budget deficit.[16] Nabiullina stated that Russia has experienced a decrease in consumer activity and that Russia’s GDP growth estimates for 2026 are between 0.5 and one percent. Nabiullina stated that the Central Bank is aiming to return the inflation rate to four percent in 2027.
The Russian Central Bank’s continued reduction of the key interest rate over an 18-month period prior to September 2026 likely contributed to domestic inflationary pressures.[17] Nabiullina has consistently expressed the need for monetary restraint — often trying to resist the Kremlin’s demands to expand capital availability for the Russian DIB and devalue the ruble to increase export revenues, despite ongoing fiscal inflationary pressures.[18] The Central Bank’s apparent success in avoiding further interest rate reductions at this time indicates that Putin has likely become more tolerant of contractionary monetary policy. Putin has recently prioritized reducing inflation to secure support amongst the Russian population by attempting to reduce the economic effects of Russian war spending, a prioritization that may have led him to accept Nabiullina’s fiscal policy for now.[19] Keeping the key rate at the current level will likely suppress wage growth and limit the amount of capital available to the Russian DIB, which may prevent Putin from achieving his goals of raising Russians’ effective purchasing power and maintaining the DIB’s production capacity. It remains difficult to assess, however, what effect fiscal policy will have on wage inflation and Russians’ quality of life, since Russia’s persistent labor shortages drive wage inflation for employed individuals while households face pressures that nominal wage figures do not capture.[20]
A likely Russian drone struck a cargo ship off the coast of Romania and drone debris fell in Moldova on October 23. Romanian President Nicusor Dan stated on October 23 that an unspecified drone struck a Comoros-flagged Khoryv cargo ship “near Romanian territorial waters” and added that the strike is a consequence of “Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.”[21] The Romanian Naval Authority reported that the Khoryv vessel sent a distress signal about 13 nautical miles (around 24 kilometers and just outside of the Romanian territorial waters) off the coast of Constanta, Romania.[22] European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the October 23 drone strike yet another “Russian escalation” in the Black Sea.[23] Territorial waters extend up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 kilometers) from the country's shoreline, and states have sovereignty and jurisdiction over their territorial waters.[24] The October 23 drone strike comes against the backdrop of recent escalating Russian strikes against vessels in the Black Sea, including likely Russian drone strikes against two commercial tankers within Romanian territorial waters on October 14 and 15 and strikes against civilian vessels in the Bulgarian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) overnight on October 12 to 13.[25] The Moldovan police separately reported on October 23 that drone debris fell up to 100 meters from a residential building near Chistelnica, Telenesti Raion, Moldova.[26] These continuous, likely Russian violations of Moldovan and Romanian sovereign territory demonstrate Russia’s increasing willingness to pursue strike tactics that may directly impact the territory of NATO or NATO-aligned states.[27]
Ukraine and Russia conducted civilian prisoner and prisoner of war (POW) exchanges on October 23. Ukrainian and Russian authorities reported on October 23 that Ukraine and Russia exchanged 270 prisoners each.[28] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Russia returned nine civilian prisoners back to Ukraine as part of the exchange.[29] Ukrainian Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of POWs reported that the October 23 POW exchange is the third stage of a combined prisoner swap that began on August 19, 2026.[30] Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets separately reported that Russia and Ukraine exchanged seven more civilians on October 23.[31]
Ukrainian officials are widely reporting continued in-motion speed restrictions on SpaceX’s low-earth orbit satellite communication technology (Starlink and Starshield) on October 23, but the situation remains unclear.
Russia and Ukraine have reportedly agreed to a limited ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast.
Russian President Vladimir Putin articulated his long-standing commitment to wider territorial aims in Ukraine far beyond Donetsk Oblast by invoking mythologized and false Russian “historical claims”.
The Kremlin appears to be increasingly adopting a more cautious monetary policy amid continued inflationary pressures, which may pose risks to wage growth and Russia’s defense industrial base (DIB).
A likely Russian drone struck a cargo ship off the coast of Romania, and drone debris fell in Moldova on October 23.
Ukraine and Russia conducted civilian prisoner and prisoner of war (POW) exchanges on October 23.
Ukrainian forces recently advanced west of Kostyantynivka.
Russian forces launched 176 drones against Ukraine overnight. Ukraine continued its long-range strike campaign against Russian military assets overnight on October 22 to 23 and on October 23.
We do not report in detail on Russian war crimes because these activities are well-covered in Western media and do not directly affect the military operations we are assessing and forecasting. We will continue to evaluate and report on the effects of these criminal activities on the Ukrainian military and the Ukrainian population and specifically on combat in Ukrainian urban areas. We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.
Ukrainian forces launched a large strike package toward Moscow City, prompting the suspension of operations at all four Moscow area airports and the evacuation of government administrative buildings. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed on October 23 that 155 Ukrainian drones targeted Moscow Oblast overnight on October 22 and 23.[32] Russian state aviation regulator Rosaviatsia announced on October 23 that Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports — all four major airports servicing Moscow City — introduced temporary restrictions.[33] A Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) channel posted an image on October 23 showing drone debris on the tarmac at Sheremetyevo Airport.[34] The channel also published footage on October 23 purporting to show balloons flying over Moscow City, purportedly carrying explosives or small drones.[35] Russian opposition outlet Astra reported on October 23 that Russian authorities evacuated the IQ-Quarter tower in Moscow City, which reportedly houses offices for the Russian Ministries of Economic Development, the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Ministry of Digital Development, and the Federal Agency for Technical Regulation and Metrology.[36]
Ukrainian forces conducted a series of long-range strikes against a Russian defense industrial facility, a chemical production plant, and administrative and military infrastructure in Russia. Geolocated footage published on October 23 shows the moment of a likely Ukrainian missile strike against the Proton plant in Oryol City, Oryol Oblast (roughly 161 kilometers from the frontline).[37] A Ukrainian OSINT channel stated that reportedly Ukrainian Storm Shadow cruise missiles struck the plant.[38] Ukrainian defense source Militarnyi reported that the plant manufactures components for the Russian S-71 Kover cruise missiles, Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.[39] Geolocated footage published on October 23 shows a Ukrainian FP-1 drone approaching the Azot UralKhim Chemical Plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai (roughly 1,585 kilometers from the international border) and smoke plumes rising from the facility.[40] Perm Krai governor Dmitry Makhonin acknowledged on October 23 that Ukrainian forces struck and damaged an industrial facility.[41] A Ukrainian OSINT channel posted footage on October 23 purporting to show Ukrainian forces striking a Russian Federal Taxation Service data center in Gorodets, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast (roughly 785 kilometers from the international border).[42] Nizhny Novgorod Oblast Governor Gleb Nikitin acknowledged on October 23 that drone debris damaged unspecified infrastructure in Gorodets raion.[43] A Ukrainian OSINT channel posted on October 23 an image showing smoke plumes near Baltimore Air Base in Voronezh City (roughly 190 kilometers from the international border).[44] The channel reported that preliminary information indicates that Ukrainian forces targeted the former Voronezh Military Aviation Engineering University and an adjacent military aircraft parking area.[45] Voronezh Oblast Governor Alexander Gusev acknowledged on October 23 that Ukrainian drones targeted Voronezh City.[46]
Russian objective: Create defensible buffer zones in Sumy Oblast along the international border
Russian forces continued limited offensive operations in northern Sumy Oblast on October 23 but did not advance.[47]
Russian objective: Push Ukrainian forces back from the international border to create a defensible buffer zone with Belgorod Oblast and approach Kharkiv City
Russian forces recently conducted infiltration missions northeast and northwest of Kharkiv City. Ukrainian forces struck Russian positions southeast of Khrypuny (northeast of Kharkiv City) and south of Nova Kozacha (northwest of Kharkiv City), according to geolocated footage published on October 20 and 22, respectively, after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions.[48]
Russian forces continued offensive operations northeast of Velykyi Burluk on October 22 and 23 but did not advance.[49]
Russian objective: Cross the Oskil River in Kharkiv Oblast and push westward into eastern Kharkiv Oblast and northern Donetsk Oblas t
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Kupyansk direction on October 22 and 23 but did not make confirmed advances.[50]
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Borova direction on October 23.
Russian Main Effort: Capture Ukraine's Fortress Belt and complete the seizure of Donetsk Oblast
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #1 – Encircle the Fortress Belt from the northwest
Russian objective: Seize Lyman and cross the Siverskyi Donets River to support a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt – assessed objective of the Russian 25th Combined Arms Army and Western Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Lyman direction on October 22 and 23 but did not advance.[51] A Russian milblogger claimed on October 23 that Russian forces are developing an offensive from Yampil (southeast of Lyman) towards Ozerne (southwest of Yampil) and Dibrova (west of Yampil).[52]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #2 – Advance on the Fortress Belt from the east
Russian objective: Advance on Slovyansk, Kramatorsk, and Druzhkivka from the east – assessed objective of the Russian 3rd Combined Arms Army and Southern Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces continued limited offensive operations east of Slovyansk on October 23.[53] Donetsk Oblast Military Administration Head Vadym Filashkin ordered on October 22 the mandatory evacuation of all families with children in Kramatorsk and Slovyansk hromadas due to ongoing Russian strikes against civilian and residential infrastructure.[54]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #3 – Advance on the Fortress Belt from the south
Russian objective: Advance on Kostyantynivka and Druzhkivka from the south and southwest, east of the Kazenyi Torets River – assessed objective of the Russian 8th Combined Arms Army and Southern Grouping of Forces elements
Ukrainian forces recently advanced west of Kostyantynivka. Ukrainian forces recently advanced in northern Sofiivka, according to geolocated footage published on October 22.[55]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #4 – Encircle the Fortress Belt from the southwest
Russian objective: Conduct a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt from near Dobropillya and Pokrovsk west of the Kazenyi Torets River – assessed objective of the Russian 51st Combined Arms Army and Central Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces recently conducted an infiltration mission in southern Dobropillya. Russian forces are operating in southern Dobropillya, according to geolocated footage published on October 22, after what ISW assesses was a Russian infiltration mission.[56] Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets reported on October 21 that Russian forces infiltrated southern Dobropillya.[57]
Russian sources continue to use likely AI-generated or AI-altered footage to make aggrandized claims in the Dobropillya direction. A Russian source published footage on October 23 purportedly showing Russian forces raising flags in Vesele Pole (north of Dobropillya and roughly 12 kilometers from the furthest assessed extent of Russian advances).[58] ISW has reason to believe that the Russian flag raising video may be AI-generated or AI-altered, which would be consistent with previous Russian information operations that use AI footage to claim battlefield advances.[59]
Russian Supporting Effort: Advance into Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Russian objective: Interdict Ukrainian ground lines of communication that support Ukrainian positions in Donetsk Oblast and envelop Ukrainian positions in southwestern Donetsk Oblast – assessed objective of elements of the Russian Central and Eastern groupings of forces
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Novopavlivka and Oleksandrivka directions on October 23.
Russian objective: Maintain frontline positions, secure rear areas against Ukrainian strikes, and advance within tube artillery range of Zaporizhzhia City – assessed objective of the Russian Eastern and Dnepr Grouping of Forces
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Hulyaipole direction on October 22 and 23 but did not advance as Ukrainian forces counterattacked in the area.[60]
Russian forces recently conducted infiltration missions west of Orikhiv. items.title: Inflation, earnings reports and the mood of consumers and the Federal Reserve fill out a busy week - WTOP News
items.summary: Inflation, earnings reports and the mood of consumers and the Federal Reserve fill out a busy week  WTOP News
items.content:
NEW YORK (AP) — A key update on inflation and its impact on consumer confidence, economic growth and interest rate policy will fill a busy calendar this week along with more big earnings reports.
They all arrive just weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections that will determine the future makeup of Congress as the U.S. economy grapples with constantly shifting global trade conflicts and a global oil shortage brought on by the U.S. war with Iran. Inflation is stubbornly high, consumers are losing confidence and the resilient jobs market is showing more signs of stress.
Here’s a look at some of the key reports coming in the week ahead.
Consumer confidence keeps falling as inflation squeezes household budgets
Americans are losing confidence in the economy as rising prices for everything from gas to groceries guts budgets. The latest consumer confidence survey from business group The Conference Board on Tuesday is expected to show that consumer confidence kept shrinking in October.
The last report showed that confidence plunged in September to the lowest level in more than a decade. The October report is expected to show confidence kept weakening. Consumer confidence is down sharply from two years ago, according to the survey. In that time, the U.S. has waged a wide-ranging trade war with much of the world, including its neighbors and closest trading partners. The uncertainty around the sudden shifts in tariffs left businesses and consumers wary about planning ahead over worries about higher costs. The U.S. war with Iran that started in 2026 slashed global oil supplies and added more fuel to rising prices.
The Federal Reserve struggles to contain rising inflation
The Federal Reserve will close out a two-day meeting on Wednesday and is expected to hold its benchmark interest rate steady following a hike at its September meeting. The central bank has been signaling that it is still worried about inflation and that it may have to continue raising rates to help tame rising costs. Wall Street still expects that one more rate hike is coming at the Fed's meeting in December.
Higher interest rates make borrowing more costly, which in turn can slow economic growth and cool stubbornly hot inflation. The Fed has to balance taming inflation with supporting the jobs market. Higher interest rates and slower economic growth could dampen rising inflation, but they could also hurt job growth at a time when the somewhat resilient employment market is showing signs of stress.
Economic growth faces the impact of stubborn inflation, weakening consumer confidence
The U.S. Department of Commerce on Thursday will release its initial report on economic growth during the third quarter and economists expect a sluggish result. Economists are forecasting that gross domestic product, which is the nation's output of goods and services, rose 1.7% from July through September. It's the first of three reports for third-quarter GDP and can be revised higher or lower.
The forecast for the initial assessment marks an easing from 2.2% growth during the second quarter . GDP growth has been slowing since the first quarter under pressure from higher oil prices fueling already stubbornly high inflation. Growth has been bolstered by a strong stock market and businesses investing in artificial intelligence technology. Households, though, have been struggling with higher costs on everything from gas to groceries eating up more of their budgets at the same time that average wages for workers stagnate.
Inflation keeps heating up as US war with Iran squeezes global oil supplies
The latest inflation update is expected to show that prices on everything from gasoline to clothing and groceries marched higher at a faster rate in September. The U.S. will release the personal consumption expenditures report, or PCE, on Thursday and economists expect that inflation jumped at a 3.7% rate, up from a 3.4% rate in August.
The PCE is the preferred measure of inflation used by the Fed, which wants to bring inflation down to its target rate of 2%. Several other measures of inflation have also moved stubbornly above a 3%. Inflation has been rising at an even sharper rate since the U.S. war with Iran started in February, essentially shutting down the vital Strait of Hormuz and stifling the global oil supply. That has prompted a surge in gasoline prices that have been a direct hit to household budgets . Higher diesel fuel costs raised the cost of shipping and warehousing goods, which businesses typically pass along to consumers.
The latest updates on retail sales show that household spending remains strong, on the surface. Much of that spending, though, is the result of paying higher costs , especially for gasoline.
Corporate earnings reports could shed light on AI investments and household spending
Investors have another busy week of earnings ahead, with reports from big names that could provide more insight on plans for AI spending and how inflation is influencing profits.
The most closely-watched reports this week are likely to be the big technology or technology-related companies that have seen their stock values surge as they heavily invest in artificial-intelligence technology with hopes for a big benefit. Google's parent company Alphabet reports its results on Wednesday, with Intel and Amazon reporting their latest results on Thursday. Analysts expect all three companies to report profit gains as Wall Street tries to determine whether their big AI investments will translate into future growth and whether their outsized stock values are justified.
A wide range of other companies will report results this week, shedding more light on inflation's impact across industries. Shipping company UPS and beverage giant Coca-Cola report results on Tuesday. Starbucks reports its results on Thursday, while oil giants Exxon Mobil and Chevron report their results on Friday.

Brent crude oil rose to a six-month high on Friday, as investors increasingly expect the U.S. to resume strikes on Iran in the coming weeks.
Brent futures gained 3.1% to close at $116.72 a barrel, the highest settlement for the international benchmark since April 29. U.S. West Texas Intermediate added 3.8% to settle at $103.27 a barrel.
Iran's army chief, meanwhile, said the country's military is fully prepared for "asymmetric warfare" after strengthening its capabilities, according to the state media agency Tasnim .
Brent added 6.2% for the week, the third consecutive week of gains. WTI advanced 2% for the week.
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. was not negotiating with Iran and something would happen "fairly soon." His cryptic remarks came as U.S. officials told The New York Times that the U.S. and Israel have plans for fresh strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
Iran-allied Houthi militants have continued to strike Saudi Arabia.The U.S. State Department has ordered all non-essential personnel to leave Saudi Arabia due to the strikes.
A drone attack targeting the Shaybah oil field Wednesday in the Eastern Region left two people dead and two injured, according to Saudi state media. At least two people were killed and eight injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday.

items.title: Qatar deal to buy U.S. natural gas shows how Iran war has redrawn global energy markets
items.summary: The Iran war is transforming global energy markets and benefiting U.S. companies, especially liquefied natural gas exporters.
items.content:
Qatar deal to buy U.S. natural gas shows how Iran war redrawn market
Once a major natural gas exporter, Qatar's shipments have collapsed since Iran attacked its production facility Ras Laffan in March.
QatarEnergy struck a deal with U.S. exporter Cheniere Energy to purchase 4 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas annually through 2054.
The decades-long contract signals that Qatar sees a risk that freedom of navigation will never return to the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran tensions, global conflicts and the impact on markets
Before the Iran war, Qatar was one of the biggest natural gas exporters in the world. After only eight months, the Gulf state is now buying supplies from its principal competitor — the United States.
QatarEnergy struck a deal Thursday with U.S. exporter Cheniere Energy to buy 4 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, annually through 2054. The purchase price is indexed to the U.S. Henry Hub price plus a fixed fee. Deliveries are expected to begin in the 2030s.
"We look forward to reliably supplying QatarEnergy from both Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi into the second half of this century," Cheniere CEO Jack Fusco said in a statement.
The gas that Doha will buy is less than 1% of the global LNG trade of more than 400 million metric tons. But "in terms of an individual deal, this is about as big as you see in the U.S," said Alex Munton, director of global gas and LNG at Rapidan Energy in Houston.
The deal signals how the Iran war is reshaping global energy markets to the benefit of U.S. companies, cementing the dominance of American LNG exporters. Shares of Cheniere and Venture Global , the other independent U.S. player, have gained 26% and 40%, respectively, since the start of the war.
Qatar was second only to the U.S. in LNG exports before the war. But shipments have since collapsed in the eight months since Iran bombed its key production facility at Ras Laffan. The attack badly damaged two production lines, taking out about 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity.
It will take about three years to repair the damage at Ras Laffan, Qatar's energy minister, Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, has said. The Persian Gulf state has declared force majeure — citing unexpected, uncontrollable events preventing contracts from being honored — every month since the March attack.
"It did give us a big blow, if you will, for our production capability for the next few years," Al-Kaabi said in an interview on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in September. Qatar is exporting "very little" LNG right now because "we can't export through the Hormuz Strait," he said.
"Very sparingly, some ships are crossing the straits but a very small amount, it's not something that would even be measurable in a percentage point," the energy minister said.
And it is far from clear what security conditions in Hormuz will look like when the repairs are done at Ras Laffan. The decades-long contract with Cheniere indicates that Qatar sees a risk that freedom of navigation will never return to Hormuz as Iran keeps attacking tankers, Munton said.
It is harder to find ways to get around Hormuz in the case of LNG because it is fundamentally a waterborne product, the analyst said.
"It's liquefied so it can be put on a ship and that requires access to seaborne routes," Munton said. "They've got to access the Strait of Hormuz. There's no other way of getting LNG to market. They're just stuck."
With its production badly damaged and Hormuz blocked off, QatarEnergy is expanding its LNG trading business through the Cheniere deal, Munton said.
It secured a $3 billion loan earlier this month from Chinese banks that could allow it to secure more U.S. LNG to honor its international delivery commitments, said Manav Gupta, a UBS analyst, in a note to clients Thursday.
Venture Global, for example, is in advanced talks with QatarEnergy to supply 3 million metric tons annually, unnamed sources told Reuters .
With the Qatar deal, Cheniere is disproving the bears' case that it will struggle to secure incremental sales which would in turn constrain capacity expansion, Gupta said. UBS has a stock price target of $340 on Cheniere, implying 18% upside from Thursday's close.
Wall Street is broadly bullish on both Cheniere and Venture Global. Nearly 90% of equity analysts who cover Cheniere rate it a buy, with an average price target of $314, implying about 9% upside from Thursday's close.
Nearly 60% of analysts recommend Venture Global as a buy with the rest rating it a hold. The average price target of $17 would amount to some 35% upside from Thursday's close.
"The U.S. once again is being called on by buyers to diversify supply," Munton said. "So much is under construction in the U.S. that you get to the point where now the U.S. is becoming disproportionately big in terms of global [LNG] market share."

items.title: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
items.summary: Around 200 emergency personnel are deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.
items.content:
Image caption, The Eagle's Nest was still on fire early on Saturday
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Difficult terrain was hindering efforts to extinguish the blaze and it was still burning early on Saturday, police said, with some 200 emergency personnel deployed. There were no reports of injuries.
The retreat, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.
He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire.
Image caption, The retreat was seen smouldering on Saturday morning
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website , external .
During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.
There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.
While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.
In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.
Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.
And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.

items.title: Deadly ‘racist’ attack in France: Are hate crimes rising in Europe?
items.summary: Monitoring group reports more Muslims in Europe face racial discrimination as 'terrorist' attack kills one in France.
items.content:
Share Deadly ‘racist’ attack in France: Are hate crimes rising in Europe? on social media
French police work at the scene after a drive-by shooting that killed one person and injured several in Trappes in the Yvelines department near Paris [Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters]
A gunman in northern France has killed one person and injured five, including a 12-year-old girl who was seriously wounded, in what authorities are calling a racially motivated “terrorist” attack.
The shooting on Friday was carried out as mounting and often violent cost-of-living protests grip the country with more demonstrations expected on Saturday.
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 San Diego mosque shooting: What we know about the victims and the attackers
list 2 of 4 After San Diego shooting, Muslim Americans aim to turn grief into action
list 3 of 4 One person killed in suspected ‘Islamophobic’ shooting near Paris
list 4 of 4 Chocolates and a chat: A peaceful response to Quran burnings in Sweden
President Emmanuel Macron called the shooting “a terrorist and racist attack”.
So what was behind this attack? And has there been a rise in Islamophobia in Europe?
About 10:30am (08:30 GMT) on Friday, a gunman drove through the towns of Trappes and La Verriere, a working class area on the outskirts of Paris with a large immigrant and Muslim population, and fired an automatic weapon randomly at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children’s playground.
The rampage lasted about 15 minutes before the suspect, identified as 39-year-old Kevin T, was arrested. Laurent Mazaury, the local MP, said the suspect told police he wanted to “kill foreigners”. He added: “I think we are facing a racist person.”
French media reported a young Black man was killed and a woman wearing a headscarf and a 12-year-old girl wearing a headscarf were among those shot and injured.
The man who was killed was identified as Pengo Bassio Wangi.
The girl, of North African descent, was shot eight times, according to her mother, and was transferred to a children’s hospital for surgery.
In a statement, prosecutors said of the five people injured, three were in critical condition.
French police cordon off a petrol station, one of the sites of drive-by shootings outside Paris that officials said were ‘racist’, ‘terrorist’ attacks [Antony Paone/Reuters] How have the French authorities responded?
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters on Friday that investigations are “ongoing but it is clearly a terrorist crime”.
Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the suspect had conspired with a “terrorist group” and added that a member of the gunman’s immediate “family circle” had also been taken into custody.
A local police chief told French media that the authorities had found an “older-style semiautomatic weapon” used in World War II in the suspect’s car as well as tear gas grenades.
The mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said the suspect was “firing at random” and wanted to cause a “bloodbath” in the communities, calling it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.
Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was “very serious” and “all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised”.
The shooting comes at a moment of great tension in France as violent cost-of-living and student protests grip the country.
French authorities are to deploy 70,000 police officers on Saturday as protests, which some far-right voices have blamed on Muslim youths, are expected to continue.
Macron released a statement on Friday calling the “racist terrorist attack” a “turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation”.
“Tonight, I have reiterated the Nation’s support for all the victims and their families,” he said on X. “I have also reaffirmed our absolute determination to continue the fight against racism, in all its forms.”
Mayor Rabeh, who has Moroccan roots, said the people targeted “could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law”.
“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country,” he said. “Her crime was probably being of colour.”
The girl’s mother told French broadcaster RTL: “How could anyone do this to a child?”
She questioned whether her daughter had been targeted because she was wearing a headscarf.
“She’s a child who was born in France, in Trappes,” she said. “She has the right to live in France, to make her life in France.”
The leader of the far-right anti-immigration National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the attack, calling it “barbaric”.
However, Muslim groups accused the populist right of creating a climate of hatred in the country with Islamophobic rhetoric. Most recently, Le Pen, who is campaigning for the French presidency, has proposed that women who wear the headscarf in public spaces should be fined.
Some members of the far right have also sought to blame Muslim young people for the violence taking place during ongoing protests, Farid Hafez, a senior researcher at Georgetown University’s The Bridge Initiative, which monitors incidents of Islamophobia in Europe, wrote in an article for Al Jazeera.
Last week, the European Parliament passed a resolution “on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network”. It was tabled by the centre-right European People’s Party and passed in a 381-167 vote with 15 abstentions.
“Symbolically, the resolution is a major victory for Europe’s right-wing anti-Muslim forces,” Hafez wrote. “It shows that the European Parliament has started abandoning any firewall against the far right as the centre right draws closer and closer to the far right.”
Rabeh said Friday’s shooting was a result of people “blaming all the ills of this society on Arab Muslims. All these comments cause deaths,” an apparent reference to the rhetoric of far-right political groups such as the National Rally. He denounced lawmakers who have made negative comments about Muslims as “criminals” who “ideologically weaponise those who are capable of committing crimes”.
The French Muslim Council blamed “the promoters of anti-Muslim hate speech who have blood on their hands”.
French President Emmanuel Macron, right, walks with Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh as he arrives for a meeting at the town hall after the drive-by shootings [Hannah McKay/Reuters] Are Islamophobic attacks on the rise in Europe, US?
In June, Amnesty International reported that Islamophobic violence in the United Kingdom has reached “ emergency levels ” with an escalating wave of hate crimes and targeted attacks, including rapes and firebombing of mosques.
The European Union’s Fundamental Rights Agency says racism against Muslims has risen in recent years and reported that one in two Muslims in Europe experience racial discrimination, especially when it comes to applying for jobs and housing.
In the UK, the monitoring group Tell MAMA reported 1,909 anti-Muslim cases last year, a 5 percent rise on the previous year, but said the true figure is likely to be much higher because many people don’t come forward.
The Council on American-Islamic Relations released a report on Friday condemning the attacks in France. It also revealed that reports of anti-Muslim bias are at an all-time high in the United States with California’s attorney general reporting a 54 percent rise in anti-Muslim hate crimes in 2025, from 24 to 38.

US plans $389M for fusion and AI chip R&D - Metal Tech News
A.J. Roan , Metal Tech News | Last updated Oct 23, 2026 11:26am 0
Four proposed CHIPS awards totaling up to $389 million would support research into fusion power electronics, AI data center semiconductors, and high-purity quartz for chipmaking.
Four proposed awards include quartz processing vital to chipmaking.
Seeking to strengthen domestic semiconductor capabilities for nuclear fusion, advanced computing, and chip manufacturing, the U.S. Department of Commerce issued four letters of intent totaling up to $389 million in research and development awards under the CHIPS and Science Act.
Beyond the processors found in computers and phones, a different class of semiconductor controls how electricity moves through everything from electric grids to high-performance computing equipment.
Used to regulate electrical current and enable power converters to raise or lower voltage, power semiconductors help manage the large electrical loads required by modern infrastructure.
Because these processes inevitably result in some energy being lost as heat, improvements in semiconductor efficiency can reduce electricity consumption and heat generation, particularly in power-intensive applications where even small reductions in energy losses can become significant.
To advance those and other semiconductor technologies domestically, the CHIPS Research and Development Office, established under the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, supports research and manufacturing capabilities aimed at reducing dependence on overseas suppliers.
"The Trump Administration is accelerating American semiconductor innovation to enhance our domestic energy and power resources," said Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick. "These investments expand domestic research, secure critical supply chains, and create high-paying American jobs."
Among the technologies receiving attention through the latest agreements are advanced power semiconductors intended for nuclear fusion and data centers, along with specialized materials used to manufacture semiconductor wafers.
Still experimental, nuclear fusion seeks to harness the same basic process that powers the sun as a source of electricity.
Working toward commercial fusion generation, developers rely on advanced electrical systems to create, heat, and control plasma, with some designs requiring rapid magnetic pulses and others using powerful magnets to contain the superheated fuel.
The challenge of managing large electrical loads also extends to AI data centers, where growing power requirements place additional demands on the systems responsible for converting and distributing electricity to computing equipment.
Alongside the power semiconductor research aimed at fusion and advanced computing, the proposed awards also extend to materials critical to chip manufacturing, including ultra-high-purity quartz used to produce heat-resistant crucibles for growing the single-crystal silicon needed to manufacture semiconductor wafers.
Under the four letters of intent, the proposed recipients and their projects are:
• Helion Energy Inc. , Everett, Washington – up to $175 million to develop high-voltage semiconductors and advanced power modules capable of rapidly switching and recovering electrical energy from the magnets driving its pulsed fusion generators, alongside domestic manufacturing and packaging capabilities.
• Commonwealth Fusion Systems , Devens, Massachusetts – up to $85 million to advance power electronics, radio-frequency plasma heating systems, embedded electronics for fusion diagnostics and radiation-hardened devices needed for its magnetic-confinement fusion technology.
• Vertical Semiconductor Inc. , Boston, Massachusetts – up to $73 million to develop vertical gallium nitride power transistors for more efficient data center power delivery and demonstrate the technology in a 2.5-megawatt artificial intelligence computing rack.
• Sibelco North America Inc. , Spruce Pine, North Carolina – up to $56 million to develop improved purification and finishing technologies for ultra-high-purity quartz, including new processing methods and a pilot facility to test materials used in crystal-growth crucibles and semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
"These CHIPS R&D awards will support breakthroughs in power semiconductor devices and critical materials," said Bill Frauenhofer, executive director of Semiconductor Investment and Innovation at the Department of Commerce. "Accelerating domestic R&D across these technologies will strengthen America's ability to convert and deliver power for the grid, advanced data centers, defense systems, and emerging fusion energy."
While all four companies have signed letters of intent, the proposed awards remain subject to final agreements. As a condition of the funding, the Commerce Department would receive minority, non-controlling, and non-voting equity stakes in each company.

Cadence named Nokia as a deployment customer for its AuraStack AI platform on the Millennium M2000 Supercomputer, targeting AI driven design automation and high performance computing.

Stock Market Today (Oct. 23, 2026): Dow tumbles following tech sell-off
This live blog is refreshed throughout the day with the latest updates from the market. To find the latest Stock Market Today threads, click here .
Happy Friday. Stocks were falling and oil prices were rising following a sharp tech sell-off in the previous session.
Markets closed mixed on Thursday, as a tech and AI-related selloff dragged down the S&P 500 and Nasdaq while the Dow finished essentially flat.
"Tech stocks got slammed amid fresh concerns about the outlook for artificial intelligence," said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst with Capital.com. "While fears about AI are nothing new, the flavor of this sell-off was starkly different. The concern pertains to capital expenditure. But rather than the risk that AI hyperscalers are spending too much, the proverbial script has flipped."
Rodda said the perceived risk now is that they are spending too little, "or more precisely, that future capex could be lower than previously thought and the rate of growth in investment could be slowing down."
"The volatility was stoked by yesterday's first batch of Magnificent Seven results," he continued. "Meta Platforms left unchanged its CAPEX guidance and provided very little color about future plans, and Tesla reduced its full-year CAPEX guidance by 20%."
"The news stoked fears, long held by market participants, that the AI investment boom may have peaked, with the pessimism leading to a broad-based sell-off across the AI ecosystem."
Rodda added that crude prices continue to hover around recent highs, as the several untenable conflicts in the Middle East risk global energy supply at a time the global energy supply chain is developing deeper cracks.
Shares of luxury goods holding company Kering, which owns such brands as Gucci and Saint Laurent, tumbled 12.4% in premarket trading after posting disappointing third-quarter earnings.
